video.title: Peripheral Vision Lets You Volley Like the Pros

classification.reason: The coach provides executable drills and cues, such as staring at one fixation on the wall while juggling and practicing volleys against a wall with a calm gaze.

problem.title_as_question: How can you use peripheral vision and proper technique to hit crisp reaction volleys under time pressure?
problem.definition: Players struggle with fast reaction volleys because they try to follow the incoming ball with central focus, take unnecessary backswings, and hit balls too far below eye level.
prerequisites: Basic volley mechanics and net positioning

quotes.text: There is something that NovakJokovic is doing with his eyes that you can copy literally tomorrow to be able to hit crisp, clean reaction volleys like this under time pressure
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: and it involves the way he's using peripheral vision as distinct from fovial vision.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: If you watch his gaze during this volley, you'll notice that at contact here, it's not even directed at the ball.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: And in fact, your processing of motion in peripheral vision is actually much quicker and much more intuitive.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: Now as that ball starts to move, he's not immediately trying to follow it off her strings.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: The gaze that you use is calm. You watch your opponent's contact and your eyes kind of rest there.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: There's a processing mode your brain uses with peripheral vision you can learn to feel and recruit here which is actually much much faster than trying to follow the ball with your focus.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: This is exactly how highle juggling works. You'll notice there's only two fixations here both the apexes of the balls.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: So, if you watch Novak's hand behavior here, you'll notice he is perceiving the ball even though his gaze isn't moving.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: All of these little adjustments, the hand adjustments, the balance adjustments, they're coming from an awareness, an observation of ball movement that is happening in the periphery.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: So, as you develop this calm gaze, you'll have that first fixation on your opponent's contact, and your eyes will just naturally flick and find the ball one more time before you hit it.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: And so, the drills we're going to talk about for developing this kind of a volley awareness in your own game are going to be really focused on peripheral vision and that first fixation on your opponent's strike.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: The reason I like this is this is best done where you pick one fixation on the wall and you stare at it while you toss the balls.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: To succeed here, see the ball hit the wall. I repeat, see the ball hit the wall. That is the most important fixation.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: The most important concept with the hands is that you are placing the racket behind the ball. You are not swinging at it. There is no back swing on a reaction or quick volley.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: might want a little bit of back swing, but watch Novak's hands. They do not go back. The hand is placed behind the ball. And then there is a tiny forward
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: You're not willing to just hover your hand there behind the ball and wait for it. You try to take a back swing, and that's when the shanks come in.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: The other thing I want you to notice is that both hands generally move together.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: So, we can see the triple bend athleticism. You see the bend at the knees, the slight bend at the hips, the balls of the feet.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: The more you try to hit the ball below your eye level, the more shanks you're going to have and vice versa.
quotes.speaker: coach

symptoms.description: Shanking the volley or mishitting when rushed under time pressure.
Taking a backswing instead of placing the racket directly behind the ball.
Hitting the volley far below eye level rather than bending down to lower head and eye height.

causes.statement: Trying to immediately track the ball out of opponent contact with foveal focus instead of maintaining a calm gaze and using peripheral vision.
Taking a backswing when time permits rather than placing the racket behind the ball and waiting for it.
Moving the hitting hand independently rather than keeping both hands together to adjust with the trunk.
Leaving eye level high above the ball instead of using triple-bend knee and hip flex to bring eye level down.

angles.summary: Novak Djokovic only makes two fixations on reaction volleys, resting his gaze at opponent contact while tracking early ball flight peripherally.
High-level juggling relies on two apex fixations while peripheral vision monitors the remaining ball flight and guides hand movements.
Fast volleys are not full swings but placing the racket behind the ball with both hands coordinated and letting the ball rebound with a tiny nudge.
Lower body triple bend allows players to lower their eye level close to the contact height, minimizing mis-hits.

solutions.summary: Pick a single fixation point on a wall and stare calmly at it while juggling balls purely using peripheral vision.
solutions.external_goal: Stare at one fixation point on the wall while juggling.

solutions.summary: Hit volleys against a wall, ensuring you see the ball clearly hit the wall and keeping a calm forward gaze during early flight.
solutions.external_goal: See the ball hit the wall with a crystal clear mental image.

solutions.summary: Place the hand and racket directly behind the ball without taking a backswing, hover and wait for the ball, then punch forward with a tiny swing.
solutions.external_goal: Place the racket behind the ball and let it bounce off.

ban_conflict.note: Prohibits taking any backswing on reaction volleys.

solutions.summary: Keep the non-dominant hand moving together with the hitting hand to coordinate racket adjustment through the trunk.
Bend the knees and hips on low balls to drop your eye level down closer to the height of the ball.
solutions.external_goal: Bring eye level down close to the ball's height.
